full_judgment:
2. The case was contested by the pre-emptee contending that the pre-emptors are strangers to the holding to which the land transferred appertains. The original jote recorded under C.S. khatian No. 21 was partitioned amongst the co-sharers and separate new jamas were created and the same were recorded in separate record of right. Opposite parties 17 and 18 claiming to be co-sharers to the holding by inheritance, prayed for pre-emption under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 3. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materials on record rejected the pre-emptor's claim for pre-emption holding inter alia, that the tenants ledger, the Register No. 11 and the new record-of-rights 37-40 indicate that 4 separate jamas were created by splitting up the jote recorded in C.S. khatian No. 21. The learned Munsif in that view of the matter, held that "the original jote under c.s. khatian No. 21 do no longer exist after conversion of it into 4 new jamas, the petitioners have no co-sharership to the case jote which falls within the ambit of record-of-right No. 40. The O. P. 1 has purchased from Khatejan in whose name stands the R.O.R. jote No. 40 and the case land also falls within that R.O.R." 

 4. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge reversed the decision of the learned Munsif and granted pre-emption in the following terms: "That the Misc. Appeal be allowed on contest with costs against the contesting respondents and exparte against the rest. The judgment of the learned Munsif is set aside. The petitioners are entitled to pre-emption along with O. P. 17 and 18". The learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the jote recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 21 continued to exist and that there was no splitting up of the jama ass contended by the pre-emptee. According to the learned Subordinate Judge the creation of the 4 R.O. R. No. 37-40" cannot be treated as a regular partition by metes and bounds". The learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the "presumption of jointness as recorded in C. S. Khatian can be rebutted only by a decree in a partition or a registered partition deed among the co-sharers or by an application under section 88 of the B. T. Act. But the O. P. No. 1 cannot produce any such paper. Thus it clearly proves that there was no partition by metes and bounds among the co-sharers of the e. s. khatian either by partition suit or by registered partition deed. 'Therefore the joint-ness of the jama recorded in C. S. khatian is still in existence." 

 7. It was next contended by Mr. Rafiqur Rahman that the record of right raises a presumption of correctness at the time when it was prepared. There is also a presumption in favour of its continuity but such presumption is rebuttable. According to Mr. Rahman the pre-emptee has rebutted the presumption arising out of c.s. record-of-right by producing the 4 record-of-rights. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman submits that the learned Subordinate Judge acted with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in holding that it is only a decree in partition suit or a registered deed between the parties that partition by metes and bounds can be effected. A partition may be effected through court by a decree or by a deed between the co-sharers. Both have the same effect. Here the question is not of partition in terms of share between the co-sharers but the question is whether the jamaas evidenced by C.S. khatian No. 21 exists or it ceased to exist giving rise to four different khatians under new record of rights 37-40. Mr. Nurul Haque Bhuiya in support of the judgment of the learned. Sub-ordinate Judge submits that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was not incorrect in the view taken by him. According to the learned Advocate a jama can be split up by an application under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in addition to the manner referred to by the learned Subordinate Judge. True, the provisions for subdivision of a joint tenancy and distribution of rent thereof have been made in section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It appears that the lands of c.s. khatian No. 21 were recorded in 4 separate khatians on the basis of specific -possession of the heirs of Abdul, the original recorded tenant. The heirs of Abdul did not challenge such possession by amicable arrangement and they have been paying rent separately in terms of the separate khatians. Evidently the amicable arrangement does not amount to partition by metes and bounds. The question of possession according to share remains open to adjustment. This question may be conveniently decided between the parties in an appropriate suit. For the purpose of pre-emption it is evident that the 4 record-of-rights separately recorded the lands of the c.s. khatian No. 21. There is no dispute that the land sought to be pre-empted is covered by record-of-right 40 and it belonged exclusively to Khatian. In the circumstances it is difficult to conclude that the original c.s. khatian is still continuing. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman has also referred to the separate payment of rent in terms of the separate record-of-rights. This is another circumstance of actual splitting up of the jamas. In the circumstances the contention of Mr. Rahman is of substance.
